context: Both diagrams show undirected graphs on vertices 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5. In a connected undirected graph, you can reach any other vertex from any starting vertex by following a path of one or more edges. The vertices need not all be directly connected in pairs.
description: The connected graph on the left, labeled “All vertices are reachable,” has seven undirected edges: 1–2, 1–3, 1–5, 2–3, 2–4, 2–5, and 4–5. Even vertices 3 and 4, which have no direct edge, can reach each other along 3–2–4 or 3–1–5–4. All five vertices thus belong to one connected component.

The disconnected graph on the right, labeled “Some vertices are unreachable,” retains the five edges 1–2, 1–3, 1–5, 2–3, and 2–5 among four vertices. The two edges incident to vertex 4, namely 2–4 and 4–5, have been removed. Vertices 1, 2, 3, and 5 remain mutually reachable, but none has a path to the isolated vertex 4.

frames.explanation: The graph on the right splits into the connected set {1, 2, 3, 5} and the isolated vertex {4}. An undirected graph is disconnected if even one pair of vertices has no path between them.
frames.title: Connected and disconnected graphs: all vertices reachable versus an isolated vertex

summary: Compare a graph in which all five vertices are mutually reachable with one that has an isolated vertex.
title: Connected and disconnected graphs: all vertices reachable versus an isolated vertex
